label: Ivacaftor: follow the evidence
title: What does the initial IND review add to the discovery paper?
stage: 2014 discovery paper compared with the reproduced 2006 initial IND review
identity: Compound 48 in the discovery chapter; VRT-813077 in the FDA review.
imageAlt: Chemical structure of ivacaftor, the nominated development candidate
question: Could this candidate improve the function of defective CFTR in human airway tissue?
rationale: CFTR dysfunction reduces chloride transport. The team’s hypothesis was that helping channels already at the cell surface open more often could restore useful function.
timing: This is a comparison of sources, not a timeline of new experiments. The discovery paper is retrospective; neither source dates each study relative to candidate nomination.

discovery.title: What lead optimization contributes
discovery.limit: The discovery paper was published in 2014, after ivacaftor received FDA marketing approval in 2012. It looks back across discovery and later development, so we cannot assume every reported result was available by the end of lead optimization or identify exactly which studies were added after candidate nomination.

source.label: Hadida et al., 2014 · Assays and profiling, pp. 9777–9781, 9793–9794

discovery.intro: The F508del potency assay was cell-based. F508del names the CFTR variant—a deletion of phenylalanine at position 508—not the assay format. Vertex ranked analogs by functional responses in engineered cells, then examined selected compounds in human airway cultures and broader profiling assays.

assays.label: CFTR potentiator potency
assays.system: Mouse NIH-3T3 fibroblasts expressing human F508del-CFTR. Incubation at 27 °C for 16–24 hours helped channel trafficking before compound treatment and forskolin stimulation.
assays.readout: Voltage-sensitive dyes on a FLIPR plate reader detected membrane-potential changes caused by chloride efflux.
assays.result: Compound 48: EC₅₀ = 3 ± 1 nM (Table 8). The paper used this assay for SAR unless stated otherwise.
assays.meaning: Ranks functional potency under defined cellular conditions. It does not measure binding affinity or show that the compound itself corrects F508del trafficking.

assays.label: Activity in human CF airway cells
assays.system: Primary human bronchial epithelial (HBE) cells from F508del/F508del CF donors, grown as epithelial layers on permeable supports.
assays.readout: An Ussing chamber system recorded short-circuit current—an electrical measure of ion transport across the epithelial cell layer—with a chloride gradient and forskolin stimulation.
assays.result: Compound 48: EC₅₀ = 22 ± 10 nM. Table 9 compares compounds 28, 30 and 45–48 in this HBE assay.
assays.meaning: Tests whether activity extends to disease-relevant human cells using an electrical readout. These are cultured cells, not a clinical measurement of lung function.

assays.label: Response in a second CF genotype
assays.system: HBE cultures from G551D/F508del CF donors. G551D substitutes aspartate for glycine at position 551 and impairs CFTR gating.
assays.readout: Ussing-chamber chloride secretion: both concentration–response potency and the maximum response relative to non-CF airway cultures.
assays.result: Compound 48: EC₅₀ = 0.236 ± 0.200 μM; maximum chloride secretion approached 50% of the non-CF level.
assays.meaning: Adds a patient-population hypothesis and a measure of response size. The authors say G551D activity guided their choice of patients to study; it did not prove clinical benefit.

source.label: pp. 9780–9781 · G551D activity and patient-population rationale

assays.label: Check upstream cAMP signaling
assays.system: Fischer rat thyroid (FRT) cells were exposed to test compound for 15 minutes, then lysed for a cAMP immunoassay.
assays.readout: Total cAMP, including cellular and secreted cAMP, quantified against a standard curve.
assays.result: The paper describes the method on p. 9793 but does not present a corresponding compound-48 cAMP result in its main results.
assays.meaning: Asks whether increased chloride transport could follow an upstream signaling change. The result summarized in the IND review is compared in the next section.

assays.label: Follow a known off-target liability
assays.system: A Ricerca assay for the GABAₐ benzodiazepine binding site. The paper does not specify the ligand or receptor preparation.
assays.readout: Binding-assay IC₅₀ for lead 16; a fixed-concentration “percent activity” readout for selected later compounds.
assays.result: Lead 16: IC₅₀ ≈ 0.1 μM. At 10 μM, compounds 36, 45 and 48 gave 47%, 52% and 18% activity, respectively (footnote 17).
assays.meaning: Tracks an off-target interaction alongside CFTR potency. A binding result does not tell us whether GABAₐ channel function is activated or inhibited; a single-point percentage is not an IC₅₀.

assays.label: Check a wider set of unwanted effects
assays.system: Compound 48 was tested in a 160-target Ricerca panel, an hERG assay and assays for six CYP enzymes. Individual assay platforms are not specified in the paper.
assays.readout: Panel activity and inhibitory potency against hERG and CYP1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 2E1, 3A4 and 2D6.
assays.result: No significant activity reported in the 160-target panel; hERG IC₅₀ > 10 μM; all six CYP IC₅₀ values > 20 μM.
assays.meaning: Broadens the selectivity profile and checks early cardiac and metabolic interaction liabilities. These measurements do not establish clinical safety or replace the later safety package.

discovery.note: Read the numbers within their assay. Cellular EC₅₀, receptor-binding IC₅₀ and a response at one fixed concentration answer different questions. The 3 nM engineered-cell result, 22 nM F508del-HBE result and 236 nM G551D/F508del-HBE result also come from different biological systems. Forskolin stimulates cAMP signaling to activate CFTR; potentiation is measured on top of that stimulation.

comparison.title: What the initial IND review adds
comparison.intro: Compare the same biological questions in the discovery paper and the FDA review. The review summarizes three submitted pharmacology reports: B227, B228 and B229.

rows.question: Does the candidate increase chloride transport?

paper.text: Table 8 reports 3 ± 1 nM potency for compound 48 in the engineered NIH3T3 F508del assay. This was a candidate result, not just evidence from a tool compound.

ind.text: B227 describes fluorescence and electrophysiology experiments in NIH3T3 and FRT cells. With forskolin stimulation, FRT-cell EC₅₀ values were 18 ± 6 nM for F508del and 36 ± 6 nM for G551D.

addition.label: Check that activity survives a different assay
addition.text: An electrical readout and another cell background help test whether activity extends beyond one fluorescence assay. Comparing CFTR variants also shows how potency depends on the biological system. This strengthens the evidence for candidate function without proving binding affinity or patient benefit.

rows.question: Does it change channel gating or upstream signaling?

paper.text: The paper describes CFTR potentiation and includes a cAMP-measurement method. Its main results do not present the detailed single-channel and phosphodiesterase findings summarized in the IND review.

source.label: Discovery paper · pp. 9780–9781; cAMP method p. 9793

ind.text: B228 reports increased channel open probability without changed single-channel conductance. The candidate did not increase cAMP in the reported assay; phosphodiesterase inhibition occurred only at concentrations much higher than those needed for potentiation.

addition.label: Distinguish channel action from upstream signaling
addition.text: More chloride transport could result from increased cAMP rather than an effect on CFTR gating. Single-channel measurements, together with cAMP and phosphodiesterase assays, help distinguish these explanations and support the proposed mechanism of the candidate.

rows.question: Does the effect extend to human CF airway tissue?

paper.text: Table 9 reports F508del bronchial-cell potency of 22 ± 10 nM. The text also reports G551D/F508del bronchial-cell activity and chloride secretion approaching half the non-CF level. Patient-derived tissue was already part of this published account.

ind.text: B229 describes F508del-homozygous bronchial cells and nasal-polyp tissue, plus non-CF controls. Forskolin-stimulated activity increased; some bronchial experiments used a corrector. In nasal tissue, glibenclamide blocked the stimulated response.

addition.label: Understand the conditions needed for a tissue response
addition.text: Human-airway activity was already reported in the paper. The review adds stimulation, corrector and control details that help explain the observed response. These conditions matter when judging whether a CFTR potentiator could work alone or might depend on restoring channels to the cell surface.

comparison.note: Forskolin stimulates the cAMP pathway; a corrector helps CFTR reach the cell surface. B229’s F508del tissue findings and the discovery paper’s G551D tissue findings concern different CFTR genotypes.
comparison.rationaleNote: The last column explains the scientific value of the evidence. The reviewed passages do not establish that FDA requested these experiments or that they were newly performed after candidate nomination.

items.label: The reviewer’s interpretation
items.text: The reviewer summarized increased chloride transport in engineered cells and human bronchial cells, and interpreted the mechanism experiments as direct potentiation of channel gating rather than an effect through increased cAMP signaling.

items.label: Requests or changes in these passages
items.text: We did not identify a request to add or repeat primary pharmacology studies in the reviewed B227–B229 passages. That does not establish what happened in every FDA interaction or mean the whole IND was accepted without changes.

items.label: What remained unproven
items.text: These experiments did not demonstrate improved lung function or establish which CF populations would benefit from treatment. Results obtained with stimulation or a corrector cannot be treated as proof that ivacaftor alone would work across CF genotypes.

takeaway: The biological case rests on the candidate’s activity, an explanation for that activity, and evidence from relevant human tissue. Whether that produces meaningful benefit in patients remains a clinical question.

sources.label: Hadida et al., 2014 · Discovery paper, pp. 9780–9781 and 9793
